name: Mud
lede: Mud is the color of wet soil, a name that has carried a faint insult for painters and a good deal of practical use for dyers and soldiers.

sections.title: Wet soil
sections.body:
Paterson's dictionary defines mud as the color of wet soil and notes that it appears among the colors of Winifred Nicholson's 1944 chart; mud brown is simply a dark brown [1]. The adjective is harsher. *Muddy* describes colors that look murky or cloudy, literally and figuratively, and "clear as mud" is an idiom for something obscure [1].

The swatch here, #735C12, is an olive brown from the 2010 xkcd color survey, and its nearest ISCC-NBS name is moderate olive brown, within a color distance (ΔE) of 5.0 [14]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary records a color called mud from 1839 [14]. Real mud ranges from grey to red to ochre, so this swatch is one common reading and not a definition [1][14].

sections.title: Paris mud
sections.body: In the middle of the eighteenth century the French began to name new shades with vivid phrases, among them *boue de Paris*, Paris mud, alongside names that invoked a pigeon's throat or a nymph's thigh [2]. Pastoureau ties the fashion to better dyeing chemistry and a wider taste for half-tones such as beiges, browns, pinks and greys [2]. In 1792 the wardrobe Marie Antoinette was allowed in the Temple prison included a chemise with a riding collar in a color known as Paris mud [3].

sections.title: Mud as a material
sections.body:
Mud has been a working ingredient for dyers for a long time. Early European black dyes from tannin-rich bark and roots held poorly, and in some regions dyers paired them with iron-bearing mud or silt, whose salts acted as a mordant [4]. Village indigo paste in India could contain so much mud, lime and plant material that its true dye content fell as low as 2 per cent, against more than 70 per cent in the best Bengal product [7]. Alkaline river mud was also one of the sources of alkali for indigo vats [7].

Pliny described indigo as a mud that clings to the foam of reeds in India, black as it separates and giving a fine blue-purple when diluted [9]. Mud also works as a resist: in Mali, mud is applied around patterns on pre-mordanted cloth to leave pale designs on a dark ground, and Balfour-Paul thinks the result may owe a debt to indigo's negative-on-positive patterns [5]. In Sindh and eastern Rajasthan, the resist paste for ajrakh and printed cloths is a clay-rich mud, made sticky with gum arabic, castor oil, lime and wheat flour and kneaded by foot, and the recipes are closely kept [6].

The best-known mud uniform is [[khaki]]. The word is Urdu for dusty, and the color is usually credited to Sir Harry Lumsden, who in 1846 had white cotton from a Lahore bazaar soaked and rubbed with river mud for his Corps of Guides at Peshawar [8]. Dusty brown uniforms dyed with coffee, tea, soil and curry powder, when no muddy riverbed was handy, spread through the Indian army between 1860 and 1870 [8]. Not all mud is brown: in 1845 a French mission brought home pots of Chinese green mud, Lo Kao, the first one-pot natural green dye, which was a paste made from two species of buckthorn [10].

sections.title: Mud in painting
sections.body:
Painters use the word for the gray-brown a palette turns into when colors are stirred together. Gurney describes two camps [11]. One says muddy mixtures are real, while the other says that only muddy relationships exist, and that drabness comes from poor value organization, not from bad mixing [11]. Delacroix is reported to have said that, given mud and the choice of its surroundings, he could make the skin of Venus [11]. Some painters scrape leftover paint into a gray paste and keep it in a tube, called mud or sauce, to lower the chroma of other mixtures [11].

The joke is old. Gage reports that Annibale Carracci laughed at an approach to color that amounted to good drawing and coloring with mud [12]. John Ruskin said he could paint a luminous picture from street mud, gravel-pit ochre, whiting and coal dust if given time to grade them [13]. The practical lesson is the painters' own: judge a mud-colored patch by what sits beside it.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, as photographed, a color within ΔE 6 of this swatch covers at least 5% of the canvas in 604 paintings, 2.5% of the archive [15]. None of the 140 Impressionist paintings and none of the 38 Realist ones qualify [15]. The 1830s stand out, with 42 of 663 paintings (6.3%, 2.5 times the baseline) [15].

Paulus Potter has it in 9 of 28 works, a rate 12.7 times the baseline of the museums his works come from [15]. By country, the United Kingdom has it in 35 of 593 paintings and the United States in 83 of 1,729 [15]. Inside a painting it is a mid-tone in 59% of cases and a highlight in 29% [15]. The strongest match is a long Ming scroll, [[painting:aic-71509|Going up the River at the Qingming Festival]], where it fills 76% of the image; Winslow Homer's [[painting:met-11123|Harvest Scene]] covers 44% [15]. The scroll's high figure is probably the aged ground, not painted earth, but a color match cannot tell [15].

It keeps company with [[olive]], [[mustard]], [[khaki]] and [[chocolate]] [15]. In printed English the adjective use of the word peaks in the 1910s [16]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a look-alike color and not a pigment test [15].

origin.first_recorded: Maerz & Paul list a color named mud from 1839; the French fashion shade boue de Paris dates from the mid-1700s

disambiguation.gloss: Urdu for dusty; first dyed with river mud, but a lighter, yellower color

other_languages.name: boue de Paris (a mid-1700s fashion shade)

questions.q: What was the mud used for in the first khaki uniforms?
choices: White cotton was soaked and rubbed with river mud to dye it dusty
It was mixed into the buttons
It was only used for boots
questions.answer: White cotton was soaked and rubbed with river mud to dye it dusty

questions.q: Some painters argue that there is no such thing as a muddy color mixture, only muddy relationships between colors.
Why did early dyers add iron-rich mud to tannin black dyes?
choices: The iron salts worked as a mordant to fix the dye
To make the dye smell better
questions.answer: The iron salts worked as a mordant to fix the dye
